doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: What New Orleans jazz funerals mean, and the funeral of Waldron 'Frog' Joseph
summary: Musicians and mourners from all walks of life set differences aside at jazz funerals; he recalls the funeral of trombonist Waldron 'Frog' Joseph.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: When you say “the people,” New Orleans has always had the most amazing mix of people.
So that’s what you’re hoping comes back.

Yeah, yeah. From all walks of life you know. If you’ve ever been to New Orleans and attended a jazz funeral in New Orleans, you know like some of the old time jazz musicians, when they pass, it’s always at that time when I attend one of those and I listen to the music, I listen to the musicians come together to play and the singers coming together to sing, and watch the people coming in from all types of walks of life. It’s then that I realize why I stayed in New Orleans all my life. That particular thing. It’s like with the music, with the musicians who come together to perform at this particular time. Ordinarily some folks might not get along as well because of human relationships or whatever, but when they put their differences aside and come together for the main purpose of just paying homage to this great musician who passed, that’s the purity, that’s the beauty of it. So if that could come back New Orleans has a good chance of going on from there, not so much to be like it was but to go on and make it even better. But those people have to come back because they’re the ones who bring that spirit and that certain thing. It’s hard to put into words but you feel it more than you could say what it is, but you feel it. And I remember like one of the last funerals I attended was a great friend of mine, an old guy by the name of Waldron “Frog” Joseph, he was a trombone player that was good friends with my father and my uncle who played trombone back then sometimes I played a lot of gigs with him like brunches. And he had some sons who also are still playing. And being there in the atmosphere of what was going on in that particular church, when I talk about it I get full.
Yeah. There’s nothing like it anywhere else I bet.
